episodes: Ep 167: One hundred starlings released in 1890 now number roughly 150 million and cause eight hundred million dollars in annual crop damage.
Ep 166: Mexico City's 1989 Hoy No Circula program prompted 85,000 annual used-vehicle imports, shifting the fleet toward dirtier cars.
Ep 165: Red-light cameras cut right-angle crashes 24.6 percent yet raised rear-end crashes 14.9 percent across 132 intersections.
Ep 164: By 2012 the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program had distributed 4.49 million hectares yet tenancy persisted on reclassified lands.
Ep 163: The 1986 Oosterschelde barrier cut tidal volume by thirty percent, leaving a four-hundred-million-cubic-meter sediment deficit.
Ep 162: Britain's 1696 window tax led owners to seal thousands of windows, darkening homes and spreading illness.
Ep 161: Over 500 native species vanished from Lake Victoria after Nile perch were introduced in 1954 to create fisheries.
Ep 160: The 1968 National Flood Insurance Act produced 25 percent more housing starts in participating communities.
Ep 159: Flight envelope protection cut fatal loss-of-control accidents 91 percent yet left pilots slower to recover when automation handed the airplane back.
Ep 158: After banning four breeds in 1991, UK dog bite hospital admissions rose 81 percent by 2017.
Ep 157: The 22 trillion won Four Rivers Project’s 16 weirs slowed flows and caused algal blooms across South Korea’s rivers.
Ep 156: The 1990 Clean Air Act gave 3.5 million extra allowances to scrubber plants, keeping high-sulfur coal units running longer.
Ep 155: The lifeboat rules passed after the Titanic sank capsized the Eastland, drowning 844 passengers at a Chicago dock.
Ep 154: In 1972 Inco built a 381-metre stack to clear Sudbury's air, and sent the sulphur elsewhere instead.
Ep 153: Over 80 percent of Israel's wastewater reused for irrigation lowered citrus yields by 20 percent after a decade.
Ep 152: Ban-the-box laws widened the Black-White job callback gap from 7 to 43 percent in New Jersey and New York City.
Ep 148: In 1988, the Philippine law meant to redistribute 4,900 hectares of Hacienda Luisita instead let owners keep control through shares.
Ep 141: James Watt's engine used one-third the coal of Newcomen engines but raised Britain's coal consumption many times over.
Ep 134: New Zealand's 1080 drops targeted possums to protect forests and cattle, yet stoats turned sharply on kiwi and other ground birds.
Ep 130: Europe's diesel tax breaks cut CO2 but filled city streets with nitrogen dioxide instead.
Ep 129: Dutch engineers drained peat wetlands to create farmland — and turned the soil itself into fuel for fires that now threaten those same fields.
Ep 128: Denmark paired generous benefits with mandatory training to protect workers, yet employers cycled them through short contracts instead.
Ep 127: Sweden's 2016 nuclear capacity tax aimed to favor renewables but triggered early reactor closures and higher coal imports.
Ep 126: The treaty that saved the ozone layer quietly accelerated global warming through its chemical replacements.
Ep 125: Kenya gave free uniforms to boost primary-school enrollment, but families redirected the savings to secondary siblings instead.
Ep 124: Soviet planners diverted two rivers to grow cotton in Central Asia, and the Aral Sea shrank by more than ninety percent.
Ep 123: Japan's rice price supports kept steep terraces farmed until aging left them abandoned to bamboo and erosion.
Ep 122: Post-Soviet Russia leased its Siberian forests for sustainable harvesting, but self-reported data turned the leases into cover for large-scale illegal logging.
Ep 121: South Korea charged shoppers for thin plastic bags in 1999 to cut waste, only to watch manufacturers switch to thicker “reusable” film that escaped the fee and raised handling costs.
Ep 120: Australia built a 1907 fence across Western Australia to stop rabbits from spreading, yet the animals had already crossed before the last wire was strung.
Ep 119: Norway introduced vessel quotas to protect cod stocks, only to watch fishers discard catches at sea to game the system.
Ep 118: Swiss subsidies paid farmers per grazed hectare to keep alpine meadows alive, yet the money quietly emptied the steep slopes instead.
Ep 117: Europe mandated biofuels to cut emissions — and triggered peat-forest clearing whose carbon releases often exceeded the fossil fuels replaced.
Ep 116: Airbags were engineered to protect unbelted adults in frontal crashes, yet the same deployment force killed children in otherwise survivable low-speed accidents.
Ep 115: Spain built high-speed AVE rail to replace short-haul flights between its biggest cities, only to watch the connecting traffic that sustained dozens of smaller regional airports disappear.
Ep 114: U.S. sugar tariffs meant to protect farmers instead pushed manufacturers toward high-fructose corn syrup, reshaping American diets.
Ep 113: Canada closed the cod fishery to protect Newfoundland stocks, then steered fishers toward snow crab — only to create a new single-species dependence that proved just as fragile.

Ep 112: Australia switched its roads to metric signs to simplify measurements and match global standards, yet the change left drivers' mental maps in miles and raised fatal crashes on remote highways.
Ep 111: E-cigarettes were created to help adult smokers quit, yet they recruited a new generation of nicotine users who had never smoked.
Ep 110: Italy's post-2009 tax credits for seismic upgrades rewarded money spent on buildings rather than measurable gains in earthquake resistance.
Ep 109: Finland's 2017 basic-income trial raised part-time work without lifting full-time employment, because the flat payment shrank the extra reward for earning more.

Ep 108: Villagers hugged trees in Uttarakhand to stop commercial logging and protect their watersheds, only to see resin-tapping quotas rise on the remaining pines and accelerate the very forest loss they had fought.
Ep 107: Poland subsidized coal-to-gas boiler swaps to cut emissions, only to see methane leaks from the new networks erode much of the gain.
Ep 106: London's 2003 congestion charge eased central traffic but pushed all-day parking into the residential streets just outside the cordon.
Ep 105: Chile's 1981 pension privatization sought stronger retirement savings but instead expanded self-employment and irregular contributions.
Ep 104: Britain taxed homes by counting their windows to avoid prying inside — and owners bricked them shut, leaving cities darker and sicker for generations.
Ep 103: South Africa's post-apartheid fishing quotas were meant to spread ownership — and instead created a larger roster of paper rights leased straight back to the established fleets.
Ep 102: Khrushchev sent tractors across the Kazakh steppe to grow more grain and instead watched the wind strip the soil away in a new Dust Bowl.
Ep 101: Norman Borlaug’s dwarf wheat ended India’s grain crises but left Punjab’s water table dropping nearly a meter a year.
Ep 100: Dutch subsidies boosted bicycle commuting by more than 40 percent, yet absolute head-injury hospitalizations rose because helmet norms did not keep pace.
Ep 99: Brazil planted fuel on its best pasture to replace oil — and the cattle walked north into the Amazon.

Ep 98: The treaty that healed the ozone layer accidentally put a climate accelerator in the world’s air conditioners.
Ep 97: Norway went electric faster than any country on Earth. Its old gasoline cars just changed address.
Ep 96: Deposit insurance stopped the bank run — then paid for a decade of thrift gambling that cost taxpayers $124 billion.
Ep 95: The 1986 ban was meant to end commercial whaling. Japan’s scientific permits turned spared minke into the catch.
Ep 94: California tried to stop couches from burning — and quietly filled a continent's bloodstreams with flame retardants.
Ep 93: Switzerland voted to phase out nuclear power — then imported German coal to keep the lights on.
Ep 92: US sugar tariffs designed to shield American farmers instead pushed the entire soft-drink industry onto high-fructose corn syrup and drove candy plants overseas.
Ep 91: France capped the workweek at 35 hours to spread jobs, yet firms kept total hours largely unchanged through contract redesign.
Ep 90: Congress passed the Jones Act to guarantee a wartime-ready American merchant fleet — and ended up with a handful of aging ships and cargo moving by truck instead.
Ep 89: The Endangered Species Act tried to shield rare wildlife from extinction, yet it gave some landowners a quiet reason to erase habitat before regulators could notice.
Ep 88: Federal student loans were meant to open college doors for everyone, yet they appear to have helped push tuition prices higher instead.
Ep 87: The Montreal Protocol healed the ozone layer with refrigerants that proved hundreds of times more potent at trapping heat than carbon dioxide.
Ep 86: Seatbelts and airbags slashed deaths per crash, yet drivers began taking more risks once they felt protected.
Ep 85: The chasing-arrows symbol was created to close the loop on packaging waste, yet it mostly turned “recyclable” into a comforting label instead of a working system.
Ep 84: American foresters vowed to extinguish every wildfire by 10 a.m. the next day — and spent a century building the fuel load for megafires.
Ep 83: Australia required bike helmets to cut head injuries, then watched cycling drop sharply and the broader safety math shift.
Ep 82: Microcredit set out to free the poor from moneylenders with tiny loans, yet scaling the model produced over-indebtedness and borrower distress in Andhra Pradesh and beyond.
Ep 81: Aquarium keepers released beautiful lionfish into the Atlantic, expecting them to vanish harmlessly—yet the fish multiplied and devoured the reefs instead.
Ep 80: US rules meant to cut smog by adding MTBE to gasoline instead contaminated drinking water across the country.
Ep 79: Cheap flights and Instagram made the world's fragile wonders accessible to millions — and then the crowds began to erode what they came to see.
Ep 78: Brazilian researchers bred a hardier tropical honeybee in 1956 — and released an unstoppable hybrid that spread across two continents.
Ep 77: No Child Left Behind promised to close achievement gaps through testing, yet turned schools into test-prep factories that narrowed what students actually learned.
Ep 76: U.S. corn subsidies meant to steady farm incomes instead flooded the food supply with cheap sweetener, feedlot beef, and ethanol.
Ep 75: Colonial officers stocked Lake Victoria with Nile perch to build a commercial fishery — and set off one of the fastest vertebrate extinctions on record.
Ep 74: Rent controls meant to shield tenants from spikes instead reduced rental supply and favored long-term residents over newcomers.
Ep 73: Open-plan offices promised collaboration but a Harvard study found face-to-face interaction fell roughly seventy percent once the walls came down.
Ep 72: Seatbelt laws saved drivers by the thousands, yet feeling safer may have led some to drive faster and shift risk onto everyone else.
Ep 71: Cigarette filters were added in the 1950s to ease health fears — and instead prompted smokers to inhale more deeply while creating the world’s most common plastic litter.
Ep 70: Reformers ended cash bail to free the poor before trial — and found that removing one flawed tool requires designing what comes next.
Ep 69: Uber set out to free drivers from taxi medallions with flexible, well-paid work — and left millions earning below minimum wage in algorithm-driven jobs.
Ep 68: Facial recognition was installed at airports to speed security and catch the right people — then the same systems started watching schools, stadiums, and protests.
Ep 67: Marketed as an indestructible shield against fire, asbestos fibers remained in lungs for decades and triggered a slow epidemic of cancer that regulators could not see in time.
Ep 66: D.A.R.E. placed uniformed officers in classrooms to teach millions of children to refuse drugs, yet repeated evaluations found the program produced little measurable change in behavior.
Ep 65: Plastic bag bans cut visible litter but drove shoppers to buy more trash liners and thicker “reusable” bags that often lasted no longer.
Ep 64: Malcolm McLean’s shipping container slashed the cost of moving goods worldwide — and emptied the working waterfronts that had sustained port cities for generations.

Ep 63: Zara and H&M set out to make runway fashion affordable for ordinary shoppers — and created an industry that now produces 92 million tonnes of textile waste a year while emitting 8–10% of global greenhouse gases.
Ep 62: Governments spent hundreds of billions fixing the Y2K bug, then concluded the threat had never been real.
Ep 61: The Royal Navy cured scurvy with lemon juice in 1795, then quietly lost the remedy as steamships and limes replaced the original practice.

Ep 60: Scared Straight sent at-risk teens into prisons to be confronted by inmates in the hope that fear would keep them out of trouble — and later studies found the programs raised their odds of offending.
Ep 59: The U.S. government paid southern farmers to plant kudzu to stop erosion — and the vine kept growing long after the crisis ended.
Ep 58: Companies adopted game mechanics to make fitness, learning, and work more engaging — and watched users chase points while real progress and well-being declined.
Ep 57: Twentieth-century engineers built dams to power the West and control floods, then spent decades dismantling some so salmon could reach their spawning grounds again.
Ep 56: Platforms promised clean feeds for users and quietly hired tens of thousands of moderators to deliver them, shifting the psychological cost out of sight.
Ep 55: US dietary guidelines urged Americans to cut fat for heart health — and watched obesity climb as sugar filled the gap.
Ep 54: The 1968 National Flood Insurance Program set out to limit building in flood-prone areas but instead subsidized far more development behind levees.
Ep 53: Park managers exterminated Yellowstone’s wolves to protect elk and livestock, then watched the rivers, forests, and beavers collapse in their absence.
Ep 52: The Federal Reserve launched quantitative easing to rescue the economy from another Depression — and ended up widening the wealth gap for a decade.
Ep 51: China's Three Gorges Dam promised flood control and clean power for hundreds of millions, yet its reservoir began stressing faults and destabilizing entire hillsides.
Ep 50: NIST's 2003 password rules tried to make systems stronger by demanding complexity and rotation, yet they trained users to create the very patterns attackers learned to exploit first.
Ep 49: Pediatric guidelines told parents to withhold peanuts until age three — and peanut allergies rose sharply instead.
Ep 48: Mao's China exterminated sparrows to protect grain harvests and instead unleashed insect swarms that deepened the Great Famine.
Ep 47: Smokey Bear urged Americans to stamp out every spark — and turned manageable forests into fuel for megafires that now consume the agency’s budget.
Ep 46: The 1978 Airline Deregulation Act promised cheaper flights for everyone — and produced an industry where four carriers now control roughly 80 percent of the market.
Ep 45: Post-war mortgage subsidies made homeownership reachable for millions of families — and built the car-dependent, racially segregated suburbs that later proved nearly impossible to change.
Ep 44: London's congestion charge cut traffic inside the zone by 15 percent — and shifted the jams and fumes to the boroughs just beyond its boundary.
Ep 43: Automakers recast streets as car space and turned crossing them into a crime, reshaping cities for a century.
Ep 42: St. Louis built Pruitt-Igoe in 1954 as a model of clean, modern public housing for working families — and dynamited the first buildings on national television in 1972.
Ep 41: Eisenhower’s 1956 Interstate Highway Act promised faster travel for all, yet in city after city the new roads accelerated the emptying of urban neighborhoods instead.
